\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 25\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Therapeutic Role of Endoscopy\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The second major role is: Therapeutic haemostasis\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Endoscopy can directly stop bleeding through:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. injection therapy,   2. mechanical therapy,   3. thermal coagulation,   4. and special adhesive agents.\u003c/h3>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 26\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The type of therapy depends on: whether bleeding is variceal or non-variceal, lesion size,\u003cbr>bleeding activity, and anatomical location.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Endoscopic Management of Variceal Bleeding\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Variceal hemorrhage is a life-threatening complication of portal hypertension and cirrhosis.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The preferred treatment for: Esophageal varices: Endoscopic Variceal Ligation (EVL)\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">also called: Band ligation\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Endoscopic Variceal Ligation (EVL)\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In EVL, elastic rubber bands are placed around bleeding varices causing:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  strangulation,   •  thrombosis,   •  fibrosis,   •  and eventual obliteration of the varix.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">According to Harrison’s Internal Medicine and Baveno guidelines: EVL controls acute\u003cbr>bleeding in more than 90% of patients, has lower complication rates than sclerotherapy and\u003cbr>reduces mortality and rebleeding.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Band ligation is preferred because it causes: less tissue injury, fewer strictures and lower\u003cbr>perforation risk compared to sclerotherapy.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Sclerotherapy\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If EVL is unavailable or unsuccessful: Endoscopic sclerotherapy may be performed.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This involves injection of sclerosants into or around the varices. Common sclerosants include\u003cbr>ethanolamine, sodium tetradecyl sulfate and polidocanol.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">These agents cause: endothelial injury, thrombosis, fibrosis and obliteration of varices.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">However, compared to EVL, sclerotherapy has higher complication rates including:\u003cbr>ulceration, perforation, mediastinitis, and strictures.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Gastric Varices and Cyanoacrylate Glue\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Gastric varices differ from esophageal varices because they are: larger, deeper, and under  higher blood flow.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Therefore: Cyanoacrylate glue injection is commonly used. The glue polymerizes rapidly\u003cbr>on contact with blood, producing immediate vascular occlusion.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 27\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">According to hepatology guidelines, cyanoacrylate is highly effective for: Gastric variceal\u003cbr>bleeding but requires expertise because embolization complications may occur.\u003c/p>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 27\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 27\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Endoscopic Therapy in Non-Variceal Bleeding\u003c/p>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 27\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 27\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Non-variceal bleeding commonly includes:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. peptic ulcers,\u003cbr>2. erosive gastritis,\u003cbr>3. Dieulafoy lesions,\u003cbr>4. angiodysplasia,\u003cbr>5. tumors,\u003cbr>6. and Mallory-Weiss tears.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Several haemostatic techniques may be used.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Injection Therapy\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The most common injection therapy is Adrenaline (epinephrine) usually diluted: 1:10,000\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Adrenaline works through vasoconstriction, local tamponade, and reduced arterial blood  flow.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Injection around the bleeding vessel compress tissues and promotes Haemostasis. However,\u003cbr>adrenaline alone has higher rebleeding rates, therefore combination therapy is usually\u003cbr>preferred.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Mechanical Therapy\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Mechanical therapy mainly uses: Endoscopic clips These clips directly compress bleeding\u003cbr>arteries or vessels. Clips are highly effective in:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. visible vessels,   2. peptic ulcer bleeding,   3. Dieulafoy lesions,   4. and post-procedural bleeding.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Mechanical therapy provides immediate vessel closure, strong Haemostasis, and lower  rebleeding rates.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 28\u003c/div>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Thermal Coagulation\u003c/h4>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 28\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 28\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Thermal therapy uses heat to coagulate bleeding  vessels.Methods include:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Argon plasma coagulation (APC),   2. Bipolar electrocoagulation,   3. Heater probe therapy.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Thermal energy causes: protein denaturation, vessel  coagulation, and thrombosis.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">APC is especially useful in vascular ectasia, angiodysplasia, superficial diffuse bleeding.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Combination therapy such as: adrenaline + clips, or adrenaline + thermal coagulation is\u003cbr>usually superior to single therapy.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Complications of Endoscopy\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Although generally safe, endoscopy may cause: aspiration, perforation, worsening bleeding,\u003cbr>sedation-related hypoxia, arrhythmia, and infection.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Risk is higher in: unstable patients, severe cirrhosis, advanced age and respiratory  compromise.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Therefore, adequate stabilization before endoscopy is critical.\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Failure of Endoscopic Therapy: Surgery and Radiological Intervention in Upper GI\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Bleeding\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Despite advances in pharmacological therapy and therapeutic endoscopy, some patients\u003cbr>continue to bleed or develop recurrent hemorrhage after initial haemostatic measures. Failure\u003cbr>of endoscopic therapy represents a medical emergency because persistent bleeding rapidly\u003cbr>leads to:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  hemorrhagic shock,   •  multiorgan failure,   •  acute kidney injury,   •  myocardial ischemia,   •  and death.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">According to Harrison’s Internal Medicine, Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine,\u003cbr>and international gastroenterology guidelines, patients with refractory upper gastrointestinal\u003cbr>bleeding require escalation to:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Radiological intervention or surgery\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">depending on: the source of bleeding, patient stability, available expertise, and underlying  pathology.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 29\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Failure of endoscopic therapy may mean:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. inability to visualize the source,\u003cbr>2. inability to achieve haemostasis,\u003cbr>3. persistent active bleeding,\u003cbr>4. or recurrent bleeding shortly after treatment.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Recognizing Failure of Endoscopic Therapy Patients who continue bleeding after  endoscopy often develop:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. persistent hypotension,\u003cbr>2. Tachycardia,\u003cbr>3. fresh hematemesis,\u003cbr>4. worsening melena,\u003cbr>5. increasing transfusion requirement,\u003cbr>6. dropping hemoglobin,\u003cbr>7. rising lactate,\u003cbr>8. or worsening shock.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">According to emergency and ICU protocols, recurrent instability after endoscopy strongly\u003cbr>suggests: Ongoing active hemorrhage and requires immediate reassessment.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Certain lesions are particularly difficult to control endoscopically, including:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>giant posterior duodenal ulcers,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>large arterial bleeding,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>gastric varices,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>malignant bleeding,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>and diffuse portal hypertensive bleeding.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Temporary Mechanical Rescue Therapy In severe uncontrolled: Variceal bleeding\u003cbr>temporary rescue therapy may be required while preparing for definitive intervention.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Sengstaken-Blakemore Tube (SBT)\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The Sengstaken-Blakemore tube is used mainly for: Massive uncontrolled esophageal  variceal bleeding\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">when: endoscopy fails, or endoscopy is not immediately available.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The tube contains:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. a gastric balloon,   2. an esophageal balloon,   3. and aspiration ports.\u003c/h3>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 30\u003c/div>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">The\u003c/h4>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 30\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 30\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">mechanism involves:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Balloon tamponade\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">which compresses bleeding varices mechanically and temporarily controls hemorrhage.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The gastric balloon is inflated first and traction applied. If bleeding persists, the esophageal\u003cbr>balloon may inflate cautiously.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">According to hepatology guidelines, balloon tamponade achieves temporary haemostasis in\u003cbr>many patients but: It is not definitive therapybecause rebleeding frequently occurs after\u003cbr>balloon deflation.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Major complications include:\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>1. aspiration,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>2. airway obstruction,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>3. esophageal rupture,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>4. mucosal necrosis,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>5. and perforation.\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Therefore, SBT should only be used:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. temporarily,   2. under close monitoring,   3. and preferably with airway protection.\u003c/h3>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Radiological Intervention\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Interventional radiology has become increasingly important in refractory upper GI bleeding.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Radiological procedures are particularly useful when:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 31\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  endoscopy fails,   •  surgery is high risk,   •  or bleeding vessels can be localized angiographically.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Trans jugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt (TIPS)\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The: TIPS procedure is one of the most  important rescue therapies in:Refractory  variceal bleeding\u003c/p>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 31\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 31\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">TIPS creates an artificial channel between  the portal vein, and hepatic vein using a  stent placed through the liver.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  reduces portal venous pressure,   •  decompresses varices,   •  and controls bleeding.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">According to Baveno and portal hypertension guidelines, TIPS is highly effective in\u003cbr>controlling refractory variceal hemorrhage and reducing recurrent bleeding.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">However, TIPS may worsen: Hepatic encephalopathy because blood bypasses hepatic\u003cbr>detoxification. Patients with severe liver failure may therefore deteriorate neurologically after\u003cbr>TIPS.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Other complications include:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. stent thrombosis,   2. heart failure from increased venous return,   3. and liver failure.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Despite these  risks, TIPS  remains life- saving in  severe  uncontrolled  portal  hypertensive  bleeding.\u003c/p>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 31\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 31\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 32\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Embolization for Non-Variceal Bleeding\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Non-variceal bleeding interventional radiology may perform: Angiographic embolization\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This involves: identifying the bleeding artery, and occluding it using coils, particles, glue, or\u003cbr>other embolic agents.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Embolization is commonly used for:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. peptic ulcer bleeding,\u003cbr>2. arterial bleeding,\u003cbr>3. Dieulafoy lesions,\u003cbr>4. tumor-related bleeding,\u003cbr>5. and recurrent hemorrhage after failed endoscopy.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The major advantage is avoidance of major surgery in high-risk patients.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">However complications may include:\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>1. bowel ischemia,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>2. recurrent bleeding,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>3. contrast nephropathy,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>4. and vascular injury.\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 32\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,
